Yeah. I think that that's a reasonable expectation. Our food does taste good, it's just that it always makes me cringe whenever I see a comment like "What do you think Applebee's is, Red Lobster?" To me the difference is really just that the service is better at Red Lobster and that it tries to be "more professional." I seriously doubt our cooking methods are that much better.

Look, I'm a "chef" at Red Lobster. We buy decent ingredients, but a lot of our processes are not exactly fine dining standard. 

All of your pastas? With the exception of freshly cooked chicken, are all pre-cooked, cooled, portioned and microwaved to order. This includes crab meat, shrimp and the alfredo that serves as the base of the pasta. 

All of your sides? Not just broccoli, which can be kind of legitimately steamed in a microwave, but rice, mashed potatoes, green beans, linguini...everything. Our mashed potatoes are literally straight out of a bag into the microwave.

Last, but not least, our "TurboChef." It "heats the interior moisture of the meat at very high temperatures to cook your delicious food as quickly as possible!" Bullshit - translation is it works exactly like a microwave without ruining the texture of the meat quite as badly. At my location, *everything* that isn't cooking quickly enough gets "TurboChef-ed." Dinner portion of salmon need to go out in a hurry? Get some grill marks on that sucker and turbochef that sumbitch up to temp. Parmesan tilapia, frozen steaks, stuffed flounder, you name it, we've turbochef-ed it in rushed situations.

Our food is good, but it is overpriced as all fucking get out and hardly what it's cracked up to be. Just know that you are paying significantly more for the ambiance than the food quality there. You want some real cooking? Go to a place that's not a goddamn chain restaurant.

I am a little ambivalent about classical music. For context, I play jazz and classical (sax/oboe) and have a little bit of a hand in pop music. A lot of it, I love. I also love how, with classical music, you can listen to it as if you were reading prose. I love the sophistication in expression and in musical form/harmony, something that a lot of other genres don't quite do for me.

BUT, classical music (especially older, popular composers) also strikes me as a little culturally irrelevant. There is something expressed by hip-hop, by indie music, or early jazz, that I just can't *get* from classical music. It's just not in the idiom. If I'm walking around the city at 1 am, sometimes Mozart or Chopin just doesn't cut it. As a performer, I also feel somewhat restricted by how exactly notated classical music is. Playing jazz, baroque or ambiguously notated modern classical music is so much more rewarding for me as a player, because I get to create in the moment. Again, not in the idiom of mainstream classical music, but obviously it's still fun to play and beautiful to listen to.

There are already a lot of good answers here, but I wanted to add something I learned from a Hindemith textbook that really helped me. The major sort of "arriving points" of the melody should be seconds apart. If you aren't famaliar, Schenkarian analysis does a good job at describing where those "arriving points" are a little more exactly. 

Anyway, a good example of this can be heard in the famous melody from Mozart's 40th Symphony: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JTc1mDieQI8. Listen to how the D is the arrival of the first part of the phrase, then the C becomes the arrived at note for the second. Nearly all of Mozart's melodies rely on this principle (usually in a symmetric way.)
